name: Rasterize vector fields to raster
desc: The script converts polygon vector layers into raster format using the geometry and attribute values of specified numeric fields. It uses a 'like raster' layer to define output extent, resolution (pixel size from X and Y units per pixel), data type (GDAL data type 5 = Float32), and nodata value (0). The output is a temporary raster layer generated via GDAL's rasterize algorithm, with no explicit export or visualization beyond the temporary output. No study area, time range, satellite data, classification, or analysis methods are present — this is a pure vector-to-raster conversion tool driven entirely by user-provided inputs. All parameters (vector layer, field(s), reference raster) are runtime user selections; no hardcoded datasets, dates, locations, or sensors appear in the code.
operators: gdal:rasterize

name: Segment lines by length and assign point counts
desc: The script segments input line features (e.g., roads) into fixed-length segments (e.g., 200 m), then spatially joins point features (e.g., crime incidents or sensors) to those segments within a user-defined maximum distance (e.g., 100 m); it outputs (1) a graduated segmented line layer where each segment is attributed with a count of associated points (e.g., 'NUMPOINTS'), and (2) a point layer symbolically linked to the nearest segment — enabling graduated thematic mapping of linear infrastructure based on point density or event frequency.
operators: native:splitlinesbylength

name: Export contours to 3D CAD
desc: The script exports vector contour lines (2D or 3D) to a georeferenced, elevation-preserving 3D DXF file compatible with AutoCAD and other CAD software. It detects whether the input line layer has Z-dimension (WKB type > 1000); if not, it uses GRASS v.to.3d to lift lines into 3D using a user-specified numeric elevation field. The output DXF is reprojected to a target CRS (defaulting to input CRS), written in a selected AutoCAD version (R2000–R2018), and retains Z-coordinates for all vertices — enabling direct use in civil engineering and terrain modeling workflows. No raster data, satellite imagery, time-series, or classification is involved; the process is purely vector-based geometric transformation and CAD export.
operators: grass7:v.to.3d -> native:dxfexport

name: Export agricultural forested or shrubland area
desc: The script exports a user-provided polygon vector layer to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'area_agricola_florestal_mato' in the 'public' schema, appending new records. It adds two fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp) and 'valor_areas_agricolas_florestais_matos' (a categorical value selected from an enumerated list via get_lista_codigos('valorAreasAgricolasFlorestaisMatos'), e.g., codes like 'A1', 'F2', 'M3'). The input must be a 2D polygon layer; no raster processing, remote sensing, or geospatial analysis is performed — only field refactoring and database insertion. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and classification methods are not specified — this is a pure vector data export workflow tied to the RECART database.
operators: qgis:refactorfields -> gdal:importvectorintopostgisdatabaseavailableconnections

name: Convert raster to PCRaster format
desc: The script converts an input GDAL-supported raster layer into PCRaster format, with user-selectable output data types (Boolean, Nominal, Ordinal, Scalar, Directional, or LDD). It uses GDAL's Translate function with specific metadata options (e.g., 'VS_SCALAR') and output data types (e.g., GDT_Float32 for Scalar) to ensure PCRaster compliance. The workflow reads the source raster via GDAL Open, applies format translation with type- and semantics-aware metadata, writes to the specified output path, and properly closes datasets. No spatial or temporal filtering, classification, modeling, or analysis is performed — it is purely a format and data-type conversion utility. Input study area, time range, satellite/sensor, bands, and geographic context are not specified in the code.
operators: gdal.Open

name: Classify river water quality from tweets
desc: The script classifies geolocated social media (Twitter) posts about rivers into n categories (default 3) based on a training dataset (.xlsx), using an external Python module 'Predictions.predict'. It reads translated and filtered tweet data from 'Data/Data_translated.xlsx', applies classification with user-specified allowed error (%) and number of categories, then generates a point vector layer ('Mapces') from the resulting histogram file 'Data/PointsHistogram.xlsx' containing xcoord/ycoord columns. The output layer is in EPSG:4326 and represents classified river observation points. No satellite imagery, remote sensing indices, or geospatial filtering by region/time is performed in the script — all processing is tabular/statistical/machine learning–based on pre-geocoded tweet metadata. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and explicit spatial filtering are not present in the code.
operators: native:createpointslayerfromtable

name: Calculate AWEIsh water index
desc: The script computes the Automated Water Extraction Index shadow (AWEIsh) using Landsat 8 Surface Reflectance bands B2 (blue), B3 (green), B5 (NIR), B6 (SWIR1), and B7 (SWIR2) from a single scene with acquisition date 2019-03-12 (inferred from filename LC08_L2SP_169062_20190312_20200829_02_T1_SR_*.tif). It applies the AWEIsh formula: A + 2.5B − 1.5(C + D) − 0.25E, where A=blue, B=green, C=NIR, D=SWIR1, E=SWIR2; then masks negative values to -9999. The output is a single-band GeoTIFF raster (AWEIsh_masked.tif) representing water likelihood with non-water pixels set to -9999. No spatial extent or geometry is defined programmatically — the calculation uses the NIR band’s extent as reference. Study area and projection are not specified beyond file paths; no temporal filtering or compositing is performed — only one static scene is used.
operators: qgis:rastercalculator

name: Convert raster to PCRaster format
desc: The script converts an input GDAL-supported raster layer into PCRaster format, with user-selectable output data type (Boolean, Nominal, Ordinal, Scalar, Directional, or LDD). It uses GDAL Translate with specific metadata options (e.g., 'VS_SCALAR') and output data types (e.g., GDT_Float32 for Scalar) to ensure PCRaster compliance. No spatial or temporal analysis, classification, or modeling is performed — only format and datatype translation. Input source, study area, time range, satellite, sensor, or bands are not referenced or inferred from the code.
operators: gdal.Open

name: Extract land surface temperature
desc: The script prepares input data for an LUHI (Local Urban Heat Island) analysis by ingesting and organizing geospatial rasters including Landsat 9 LST (Land Surface Temperature), DEM, land cover (DWV1), soil texture, canopy height, hydrologic soil group, and LCZ (Local Climate Zone) layers. It extracts EPSG from the Landsat filename to auto-generate standardized output filenames (e.g., 'LST_32632.tif'), reorganizes input files into 'Data' and 'Results' subfolders, sets the calculation extent by reprojecting the Landsat raster’s bounding box to EPSG:4326, and collects user-defined field names for attribute mapping. The final output is a parameter dictionary passed to ExtractionDuFichierCsvPourOutilIa — an algorithm that converts these rasters into a CSV table for downstream IA (AI/ML) tool use. No time-series or temporal aggregation is performed; the Landsat 9 image is treated as a single static snapshot. Study area is inferred from folder naming ('city' extracted from parent directory name, e.g., 'Paris_2023_32632'), but no explicit city or region is hardcoded. Data sources are all local file paths (not GEE asset IDs), so satellite metadata is derived only from filename conventions (e.g., 'LST_32632.tif') and UI labels ('Image LandSat 9').
operators: QgsCoordinateTransform -> QgsCoordinateTransform.transformBoundingBox

name: Detect agricultural and SAP areas
desc: The script detects agricultural areas and SAP (likely 'Sistemas Agroflorestais' or 'Sistemas de Agricultura de Precisão') from a precomputed COSsim raster dataset ('COSsim_2020_N3_v1_TM06.tif'). It crops the raster to a user-defined UTM-extent (ext = (-57000, -90000, -54000, -89000)), derives binary masks for agriculture (cossim // 100 == 2) and SAP (cossim ∈ {311, 322}), applies circular convolution kernels (e.g., diameter 11, radius 5) to smooth and aggregate these masks, and then combines them using thresholded logical conditions (e.g., fagr > 5/Nref, fsap > 2/Nref, pmin < fsap+fagr ≤ pmax) to produce a final binary map of co-located agricultural–SAP zones. Outputs include two matplotlib visualizations: (1) side-by-side grayscale plots of raw agri/sap masks; (2) four subplots showing convolved+combined results under varying kernel sizes (5×5, 7×7) and iteration depths (7, 9, 11), all rendered with 'viridis' colormap. No GEE server-side export is performed — all processing is local using GDAL, rasterio, NumPy, and matplotlib. The study area is a small UTM-projected region in Portugal (inferred from folder path 'C:\Users\mlc\OneDrive - Universidade de Lisboa\...'), and the input raster is a classified thematic map (not raw satellite imagery), with no satellite, sensor, or band information present in the code.
operators: gdal.Warp

name: Convert ground overlay to GeoTIFF
desc: The script converts a georeferenced raster image (e.g., from KML/KMZ GroundOverlay) into a properly georeferenced GeoTIFF file using GDAL's translate tool. It supports two modes: (1) axis-aligned georeferencing via bounding box (north/south/east/west lat/lon) with EPSG:4326 spatial reference, and (2) rotated georeferencing using four ground control points (GCPs) derived from rotating the bounding box corners around its center point by a user-specified angle. Outputs include a GeoTIFF with embedded geotransform, projection (EPSG:4326), and optional GDAL creation options.
operators: gdal:translate -> gdal:translate

name: Estimate service supply density
desc: The script converts service point-of-interest (POI) vector data into a continuous supply intensity surface using kernel density estimation (quartic kernel) with a user-defined radius and cell size, then clips the resulting heatmap raster to a study area boundary polygon. The input supply_pois is a QgsVectorLayer of service locations (e.g., clinics, schools, shops), with no temporal filtering or satellite-derived inputs; analysis is purely spatial and static. The output is a clipped, georeferenced GeoTIFF raster layer named 'Supply_DensityRaster', representing raw kernel density values (counts per unit area) within the study area extent. All parameters (radius, cell_size, extent) are derived from runtime arguments and the study_area_layer geometry; no time dimension, satellite data, bands, or classification methods are involved.
operators: qgis:heatmapkerneldensityestimation -> gdal:cliprasterbymasklayer

name: Modify land cover by name
desc: The script modifies a land cover raster by overwriting pixel values within user-defined polygon areas with a new land cover code, determined by matching a user-provided land cover name (e.g., 'Urban') against a custom lookup table containing 'lc_name' and corresponding integer 'lc_value' fields. It first clips the input raster to its own extent (effectively copying it), then rasterizes the input vector polygons onto that copy using the matched lc_value as the burn-in value, producing a modified land cover raster where overlapping pixels are replaced.
operators: gdal:cliprasterbyextent -> gdal:rasterize_over_fixed_value

name: Modify land cover raster
desc: The script modifies pixels in an input land cover raster (e.g., NLCD or C-CAP) within polygon areas defined by a vector layer, overwriting them with a user-selected land cover class value (e.g., 'Developed, High Intensity' → value 24). It first clips the input raster to preserve its extent and data type, then rasterizes the input vector polygons using a fixed land cover code derived from CSV-sourced NLCD/C-CAP classification coefficients. The output is a modified land cover raster where overlapping pixels are replaced with the selected class’s numeric code. No time-series analysis, spectral computation, or classification modeling is performed — it is a deterministic spatial overwrite operation. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code; the algorithm is generic and data-source-agnostic, relying solely on user-provided raster and vector inputs and local CSV coefficient files.
operators: gdal:cliprasterbyextent -> gdal:rasterize_over_fixed_value

name: Convert multipoint to convex hull
desc: The script converts a vector layer containing multipoint geometries into convex hull polygons (minimum bounding geometry of type 'convex hull') by first decomposing multipoint features into single-point features, then computing the minimum bounding geometry for each group of points. It outputs a polygon vector layer where each polygon represents the convex hull enclosing all points belonging to the original multipoint feature.
operators: native:multiparttosingleparts -> qgis:minimumboundinggeometry

name: Compute median elevation per grid cell
desc: The script computes the median elevation value within each polygon of a vector grid layer, using a DSM (Digital Surface Model) raster masked by a binary mask layer. It first multiplies the DSM and mask rasters (pixel-wise) to retain only DSM values where mask = 1 (null or 0 areas become 0 or NoData), then performs zonal statistics (median only) over the grid polygons, and finally replaces any resulting null median values in the grid’s attribute table with 0. The output is the modified grid vector layer with a new field 'med_median' containing the median masked elevation per cell.
operators: gdal:rastercalculator -> qgis:zonalstatistics

name: Compute largest empty circle
desc: The script computes the Largest Empty Circle (LEC) for a given point layer — i.e., the largest possible circle that can be inscribed in the convex hull of the point set without containing any input points in its interior. It first calculates the LEC center and radius using a Voronoi-based geometric algorithm (imported from becagislibrary.voronoi), then adjusts the radius for geographic CRS by converting meters to degrees using Gaussian mean Earth radius approximation, and finally outputs two vector layers: (1) a point feature representing the LEC center (with duplicate geometries removed), and (2) a buffered polygon (circle) centered at that point with radius equal to the LEC radius (64-segment approximation, dissolved).
operators: qgis:deleteduplicategeometries -> native:buffer

name: Convert ordered points to polygon boundaries
desc: The script converts multiple point layers—each containing an integer 'order' field specifying vertex sequence—into closed polygon geometries by first constructing closed paths (using 'Points to Path' with ORDER_FIELD) and then converting those paths into polygons (using 'Lines to Polygons'). The resulting polygon layers are grouped under a new layer group named OUTPUT_GROUP_NAME. Input layers must reside in a pre-existing group (GROUP_NAME), and each point layer is processed independently while preserving its original name.
operators: native:pointstopath -> qgis:linestopolygons

name: Compute slope from DEM
desc: The script computes slope rasters from pre-generated DEM GeoTIFF files. It first assigns the CRS EPSG:32129 (NAD83 / Pennsylvania South) to each input DEM using 'gdal:assignprojection', then runs 'gdal:slope' to generate slope rasters in degrees. Input DEMs are located in a Windows filesystem path containing 'pennsylvania_michaux' and 'laz_utm_0-597', indicating they were derived from LiDAR point clouds processed via CloudCompare and reprojected to UTM. The outputs are slope GeoTIFFs written to a dedicated output directory, named with the prefix 'slope_' followed by the original DEM filename stem (e.g., 'slope_laz_utm_0-597_...tif'). No classification, time-series analysis, or satellite imagery is involved — only deterministic raster geoprocessing on locally stored DEMs.
operators: gdal:assignprojection -> gdal:slope

name: Load cadastral boundary layers
desc: The script loads WMS raster layers representing cadastral parcel boundaries (specifically the 'CLOTURE' layer) for French communes, using INSEE codes extracted from an input vector layer of communes. It constructs WMS URLs targeting the French Cadastre WMS service (inspire.cadastre.gouv.fr/scpc/[INSEE_code].wms), configures parameters including CRS (EPSG code), image format, layer name ('CLOTURE'), and legend settings, then adds each valid WMS layer to the QGIS project under names like 'Cloture_[commune_name]_[INSEE_code]'. The output consists of multiple loaded WMS raster layers — not exported files — visualizing cadastral enclosure/parcel boundary geometry. No temporal data, classification, or processing is performed; it is a dynamic map service ingestion workflow. Study area: France (implied by INSEE codes and cadastre.gouv.fr domain). Data source: French national cadastral WMS service. Time range: not specified. Spatial extent: determined per commune geometry in input vector layer. Output layers are temporary QGIS raster layers added to the project's layer tree.
operators: QgsProcessingContext.LayerDetails

name: Extract municipality-scale topographic rasters
desc: The script extracts municipality-scale digital elevation model (DEM) rasters by clipping the NASA SRTM NASADEM GeoTIFF to individual municipal boundaries from the 'BR_Municipios_2023.shp' shapefile. It loads a single static DEM raster ('srtm_nasadem.tif'), filters a national municipal boundary layer for three specific municipalities in Brazil — 'Torres', 'Mampituba', and 'Itati' — and performs vector-masked raster clipping (gdal:cliprasterbymasklayer) for each, producing three georeferenced GeoTIFF outputs named '<municipio>_recorte.tif'. The study area is explicitly limited to these three coastal municipalities in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. No temporal analysis is performed; the input DEM is a static, non-temporal product. Outputs are loaded as raster layers into QGIS and saved to disk.
operators: gdal:cliprasterbymasklayer

name: Compute slope from DEM
desc: The script computes slope rasters from pre-generated Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) in GeoTIFF format, using GDAL's slope algorithm. It first assigns the EPSG:26918 (NAD83 / UTM zone 18N) coordinate reference system to each input DEM (though the DEMs are already reprojected per the comment 'Run after CloudCompare has created DEMs' and path 'reprojected/laz_utm_...'), then runs gdal:slope with default parameters (vertical units matching horizontal, no edge computation, Zevenbergen=False) to generate slope-in-degree GeoTIFFs. Output files are named 'slope_<basename>_utm.tif' and saved to a dedicated slope directory per batch group (e.g., '1600-2199').
operators: gdal:assignprojection -> gdal:slope

name: Visualize hurricane wind field and track
desc: The script generates a static PNG/JPEG layout map from a QGIS project that overlays a hurricane wind field raster (PNG) and a hurricane track vector layer (CSV) onto a base map. The hurricane wind field is styled using a categorized QML style ('hurricane_cat_raster.qml'), and the track is styled with a line-based QML ('hurricane_track.qml'). The layout extent is automatically set to the bounding box of the non-base-map layer (i.e., raster or track), reprojected from WGS84 (EPSG:4326) to Web Mercator (EPSG:3857). Legend items are customized: the raster layer is renamed to "[HurricaneName] [Year] Wind Field" and its legend node order is fixed to indices [2–7]; the track layer is renamed to "[HurricaneName] [Year] Track" (if forecasts excluded) and its legend node order set to [0]; the base map layer is removed from the legend. The final output is a cropped, timestamped JPEG file (e.g., 'larry2021_100x100_2023-10-05T142000Z.jpeg') saved in the data directory. Input data paths are derived from a hurricane file base string (e.g., 'LARRY_2021_100x100'), implying hurricane name, year, and spatial resolution — but no geospatial processing (e.g., reprojection, resampling, classification) is performed in this script; it is purely cartographic export using precomputed raster and vector assets. Study area and time range are not specified in the code — only hurricane metadata (name/year/resolution) is parsed from the input string.
operators: QgsProject.read -> QgsCoordinateTransform.transformBoundingBox

name: Download cadastral parcel data
desc: The script downloads and processes cadastral vector data from the Danish Datafordeler API, specifically targeting one of 20 predefined cadastral entity types (e.g., 'Jordstykke', 'Matrikelskel', 'BygningPaaFremmedGrundFlade') in either current, bitemporal, or temporal version. It performs an HTTP GET request to retrieve a GeoPackage (.gpkg) file, unzips it (via a custom 'Unzipper' script), and extracts all features (using expression '1=1') into a QGIS feature sink. The output is a vector layer containing the full geometry and attributes of the selected entity — no spatial subsetting, temporal filtering, or attribute transformation is applied. Study area is Denmark (inferred from 'datafordeler.dk', 'Matriklen', and entity names like 'Ejerlav', 'Sogn', 'Kommune'); time range is determined by the 'type' parameter ('current', 'bitemporal', 'temporal') but no explicit dates are hardcoded; data source is the Danish national cadastre (Matriklen2), delivered via REST API; no satellite, sensor, or spectral bands are involved — this is authoritative vector cadastral data.
operators: native:filedownloader -> native:extractbyexpression

name: Detect burned area severity
desc: The script computes the differenced Normalized Burn Ratio (dNBR) from pre- and post-fire NIR and SWIR raster layers to identify burned areas. It calculates NBR for both time periods using the formula (NIR − SWIR)/(NIR + SWIR), then computes dNBR as a binary mask where (NBR_before − NBR_after) ≥ user-defined threshold (default 0.1); this binary raster is polygonized and filtered to retain only pixels classified as burned (DN = 1), outputting a vector layer of fire scar polygons.
operators: native:modelerrastercalc -> native:modelerrastercalc -> native:modelerrastercalc -> gdal:polygonize -> native:extractbyattribute

name: Calculate contour grid statistics
desc: The script computes per-sample-no statistical summaries (e.g., mean, min, max, std, quantile, median, mode, kurtosis, skew) across a user-provided list of vector polygon contour grids. It requires all input grids to share the same 'Sample_No_' integer field and identical numeric attribute fields (e.g., elevation, depth, or model output values). For each unique Sample_No_, it aggregates values from corresponding polygons across all grids, computes the selected statistic per attribute, and outputs a new polygon layer where each feature represents one sample ID and contains the computed statistics as attributes. The geometry is inherited from the first input grid. No raster data, satellite imagery, time-series filtering, or spatial interpolation is performed — the operation is purely tabular aggregation over aligned vector contours.
operators: QgsFeature.setGeometry -> QgsFeature.setAttributes -> QgsFeatureSink.addFeature

name: Set Z coordinate from DEM
desc: The script replaces the Z (elevation) coordinates of 3D vector features (points, lines, or polygons) in an input vector layer with elevation values sampled from a user-provided Digital Elevation Model (DEM) raster at each feature’s XY location, optionally applying a constant vertical offset. It preserves original geometry XY positions while updating only the Z component per vertex using nearest-neighbor sampling from the DEM band (band 1), and supports processing either all features or only selected ones; output is the in-place edited vector layer with updated 3D geometry.
operators: native:fieldcalculator -> native:setzfromraster -> qgis.core.QgsVectorLayer.changeGeometry -> qgis.core.QgsVectorLayer.getSelectedFeatures -> qgis.core.QgsVectorLayer.changeGeometry

name: Aggregate clipped map area by administrative unit
desc: The script clips multiple input vector layers (e.g., land use or risk maps) to a user-defined mask polygon, intersects the clipped layers with administrative units (e.g., municipalities), computes the area (in km²) of overlapping geometries, and aggregates the total area per administrative unit (grouped by ISTAT code), joining results across scenarios (e.g., 'alta', 'media', 'bassa') as separate columns into a final vector layer where each row is an administrative unit and columns include ISTAT, Comune, Provincia, and scenario-specific area sums.
operators: gdal:clipvectorbypolygon -> native:intersection -> native:fieldcalculator -> native:aggregate -> native:joinattributestable -> native:joinattributestable

name: Translate raster layer
desc: The script performs format conversion and geospatial preprocessing of raster layers, including band subsetting (by index or spectral matching via center wavelength), spatial clipping (by extent or pixel window), resampling (with configurable algorithms), data scaling/offset application, no-data value handling, data type conversion, metadata copying (GDAL and spectral ENVI domain), style transfer, and optional ENVI header generation. It uses GDAL Translate or Warp depending on CRS alignment and resampling requirements, and supports exclusion of bad bands using BBL metadata. The output is a processed GeoTIFF (or other GDAL-supported format) raster layer with user-specified properties.
operators: QgsRasterLayer.bandCount -> gdal.Open -> GDALDataset.SetGeoTransform -> gdal.Warp -> gdal.Open

name: Aggregate irrigation water demand variables
desc: The script creates a time series of aggregated statistics (e.g., mean, sum) for a selected hydrological or agronomic variable (e.g., irrigation demand, evapotranspiration) from IdrAgra model output files, using user-defined vector aggregation zones (e.g., irrigation districts or water user associations). It parses the IdrAgra parameter file (*.txt) to extract simulation metadata (start/end dates, monthly flag, input/output paths), reads gridded domain and meteo data (e.g., *.asc, *.dat files), performs zonal aggregation via an internal 'IdragraGroupStats' algorithm, and outputs a vector table with fields: 'timestamp' (daily or monthly date), 'wsid' (water source/zone ID), and 'recval' (aggregated value). The time series is constructed by distributing values across days/months based on IdrAgra’s timestep logic (e.g., uniform distribution between consecutive timestamps), using cell size from the domain.asc raster for unit conversion (e.g., mm → m³). No satellite or remote sensing data is used — inputs are strictly model-derived ASCII grids and tabular meteo files. Study area, coordinate system, and exact spatial extent are not specified in the code.
operators: qgis.core.QgsVectorLayer.uniqueValues -> QgsFeatureSink.addFeature -> QgsFeatureRequest.setFlags

name: Identify hydro network monitoring points
desc: The script computes intersection points between a line layer representing the affected hydro network and the boundary lines derived from watershed or administrative management polygon boundaries. It converts the input polygons to lines, performs line-line intersection to locate where the hydro network crosses administrative/watershed boundaries, then adds X/Y coordinate fields to the resulting point geometry. The output is a vector point layer ('Monitoring points') containing the geographic coordinates of these crossing locations, intended for field monitoring of alien species along hydrological networks at jurisdictional boundaries.
operators: native:polygonstolines -> native:lineintersections -> native:addxyfields

name: Compute canopy height from GEDI and DEM-derived ground surfa
desc: The script computes canopy height as the difference between a canopy surface raster and a ground surface raster (e.g., digital terrain model), clamping negative values to zero. It then merges the resulting canopy height raster with optional GEDI raster input (likely waveform or RH metrics) and converts all merged raster pixels to vector points, assigning the pixel value (canopy height or merged band value) as an attribute. The final output is a point vector layer where each point represents a raster cell centroid and carries the computed canopy height (or merged value) in the 'VALUE' field.
operators: qgis:rastercalculator -> gdal:merge -> native:pixelstopoints

name: Detect forest stand clearing change
desc: The script computes two raster outputs quantifying forest structural change between two versions of a forest stand map (TBk): (1) 'change_DG' — a categorical raster encoding four canopy presence states (no canopy→no canopy=1, no→yes=2, yes→no=11, yes→yes=12) derived from binary dominant layer (DG) rasters; (2) 'change_DG_hdom' — an enhanced change raster that flags stands ≥ hdom threshold (default 25 m) where height reduction exceeds a negative difference threshold (default 7 m) as 'cleared' (value 100), otherwise retains the original change_DG code or sets to 0 if below hdom threshold. Workflow involves rasterizing hdom attributes from old and new stand boundary vector layers, aligning extents via intersect, and applying GDAL raster calculator expressions with conditional logic to derive both outputs.
operators: gdal:rastercalculator -> gdal:rasterize -> gdal:rasterize -> gdal:rastercalculator

name: Fetch Japanese population data
desc: The script fetches and rasterizes municipal-level population statistics for Japan using the e-Stat API (Japan's official statistics portal). It computes JIS standard 5th-level mesh codes (20m × 20m resolution in lat/long, but derived from 1/4° × 1/6° base mesh) covering the user-specified extent, groups them into 1st-level mesh codes (corresponding to ~80 km × 80 km blocks), queries the e-Stat REST API with statsDataId mapped from a local lookup file (estatId_mesh_list.txt), parses JSON responses containing population values per mesh code, converts mesh codes to centroid coordinates (using cal_meshcode5 and meshcode_to_latlong), creates a point vector layer with 'population' attribute, and rasterizes it at fixed resolution (7.5″ latitude × 11.25″ longitude ≈ 230 m × 230 m at equator) into a single-band integer raster output. The final product is a pseudo-colored population density raster with opacity 0.5 and a diverging color ramp (light purple to dark red), rendered automatically post-processing. Study area is defined by user input extent; no temporal filtering is applied — the API returns the latest published dataset for each mesh. Data source is statistical (not remote sensing), and CRS handling includes optional reprojection via TARGET_CRS and FETCH_CRS (default EPSG:6668, JGD2011 / Japan Plane Rectangular CS VIII).
operators: QgsFeature.setGeometry -> QgsVectorDataProvider.addFeatures -> QgsRasterDataProvider.bandStatistics -> gdal:rasterize

name: Import LAS point cloud to PostgreSQL
desc: The script imports one or more LAS/LAZ point cloud files into a PostgreSQL database with the PointCloud extension enabled, using PDAL's writers.pgpointcloud pipeline. It validates and executes the PDAL pipeline, then creates a vector layer (QgsVectorLayer) representing the spatial extent (bounding box polygon) of each imported LAS file as a feature in a QgsFeatureSink output. The output is a single vector layer containing one polygon per input LAS file, derived from the LAS header's min/max X/Y coordinates. No raster, classification, or time-series analysis is performed; the workflow is purely data ingestion and metadata-driven spatial footprint generation.
operators: QgsDataSourceUri.setDataSource -> QgsGeometry.fromWkt -> QgsFeature.setGeometry -> QgsFeatureSink.addFeature

name: Rasterize and fill linear or isolated environmental features
desc: The script converts linear or isolated vector-based environmental features (e.g., rivers, roads, protected areas, settlements) into a standardized raster layer for Maxent modeling. It first clips the input vector layer to territorial influence boundaries, then rasterizes it using a specified numeric field and user-defined pixel resolution, fills NoData cells with a user-controlled fill value, and finally masks the result to the spatial extent of a reference raster—producing a ready-to-use, spatially constrained environmental variable raster aligned with Maxent requirements.

name: Retract line endpoints
desc: The script retracts (shortens) the start and end segments of input line features by specified distances. It computes vertex offsets between original and extended lines, then calculates new first and last vertex coordinates to produce a modified line geometry where the start and end portions are removed—effectively 'retracting' the line inward along its direction. The output is a vector line layer with retracted geometries, supporting only single-part (non-multi-part) lines.

desc: The script rasterizes a categorical environmental vector layer (e.g., land cover, habitat type, or administrative zoning) into a standardized-resolution raster aligned to a territorial boundary mask, specifically for Maxent species distribution modeling. It first clips the input vector layer to a territorial influence boundary using spatial intersection, then rasterizes the clipped features using a specified numeric field (categorical ID), and finally masks and resamples the resulting raster to match the extent, resolution, and geometry of the provided territorial limits layer — ensuring pixel alignment and NoData handling suitable for ecological niche modeling.

name: Calculate polygon overlap density
desc: The script computes the spatial density of overlapping polygons in a vector layer by performing a union operation to split all intersecting polygons into non-overlapping atomic parts, then aggregates each resulting geometry to count how many original input polygons contributed to it (NUMPOINTS), optionally listing their unique IDs (ID_LIST); finally, it filters out parts where the overlap count is below a user-defined threshold, outputting a cleaned polygon layer where each feature represents a spatially distinct zone with its associated overlap count and optional source ID list.

name: Compute building morphology parameters
desc: The script computes a suite of geometric and morphological parameters for building polygons, including centroid coordinates (x, y), area, perimeter, shape index (perimeter/(4*sqrt(area))), detour (convex hull perimeter), detour index (perimeter/convex hull perimeter), range (diameter of minimal enclosing circle), range index (normalized compactness ratio), bounding box width and height (lengh is a typo for length), vertex count (pnt_count), exchange (area of intersection between building and its inscribed circle), exchange_index (exchange/area), and perimeter_index (building perimeter / inscribed circle perimeter). It first reprojects the input building layer to a user-specified CRS (default EPSG:5931), then refactors fields to compute all metrics as new attributes, and finally exports the enriched feature layer to an Excel or ODS spreadsheet.

name: Compute passive visibility zones from viewpoints
desc: The script computes passive visibility zones (i.e., areas visible *from* each observer point) and depth-below-horizon (DBH) rasters using a digital elevation model (DEM) and a set of observer points with unique 'ID' attribute. It first generates viewpoint features via the 'Choucas:Création de point de vue' algorithm (likely extending observer locations with azimuth/elevation sampling), then iteratively runs 'Choucas:Calcul de la vision active, passive et le raster depth below horizon...' for each viewpoint to produce per-point passive visibility rasters (binary or Boolean-like, as multiplied in raster calculator) and DBH rasters. Finally, it multiplies all passive visibility rasters together (using GDAL Raster Calculator) to obtain a composite raster where pixel value = 1 only where *all* viewpoints share mutual visibility — i.e., intersection of passive visibility zones. Outputs include: (1) a vector layer of generated viewpoints ('OUTPUT_VIEWPOINTS'), (2) individual DBH and passive visibility GeoTIFFs per viewpoint stored in the specified output folder, and (3) a concatenated raster 'Concatenation_Visi_Passive_Pts.tif' representing the spatial intersection of all passive visibility zones. No satellite imagery, time series, or classification is involved; input is strictly static terrain (raster DEM) and observer point geometry. Study area, time range, and satellite data sources are not specified in the code.

desc: The script implements a QGIS plugin tool that searches for Polish geographic locations (e.g., cities, administrative units) using GUGiK's UUG geocoding service (http://services.gugik.gov.pl/uug/), parses returned WKT geometries and attributes (name, type, voivodeship, county, commune, x/y coordinates), and adds the selected location as a feature to a memory vector layer named 'UUG_obiekty_fizjograficzne' in EPSG:2180. It supports duplicate detection by coordinates, zooms to the added feature, and uses a custom QML style. The workflow includes UI interaction (line edit input, list view selection), HTTP GET requests, JSON parsing, WKT geometry creation, attribute assignment, layer management via QgsProject and QgsLayerTreeGroup, and coordinate transformation for canvas zooming.

name: Estimate service supply density
desc: The script converts service point-of-interest (POI) vector data into a continuous supply intensity surface using kernel density estimation (quartic kernel) with user-specified radius and cell size, then clips the resulting heatmap raster to a study area boundary. It applies a custom red-to-green pseudo-color ramp renderer (Red=low supply, Green=high supply) for visualization. Inputs include a QgsVectorLayer of service POIs (e.g., clinics, schools), analysis radius (m), cell size (m), and a QgsVectorLayer defining the study area boundary. No satellite imagery, temporal filtering, or classification is performed — the method is purely spatial point-density modeling using QGIS processing algorithms ('qgis:heatmapkerneldensityestimation' and 'gdal:cliprasterbymasklayer'). Output is a styled, clipped QgsRasterLayer named 'Supply_DensityRaster'.

desc: The script implements a GIS-based cadastral parcel assignment workflow within a QGIS desktop application. It enables users to select parcels from a spatial layer (loaded from SHP files in ZIP archives), preview them in a map canvas (EPSG:31259, BMN M34), and assign them to legal acts ('Akt') via a dialog that captures shared attributes (e.g., AWB status, legal basis, annotations). The core data model includes BGst (parcels), BGstEz (survey editions), BGstVersion (geometry + metadata per edition), BGstEigentuemer (owners), BGstNutzung (land uses), and BGstZuordnung (assignment links). Data ingestion involves parsing CSV files (Grundstuecke_V2.csv, Eigentuemer.csv) and SHP geometries from ZIP archives, transforming coordinates to EPSG:31259, and upserting records into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database with conflict resolution based on KG_EZ and KG_GST identifiers and 'datenstand' timestamps. Outputs include updated database tables, synchronized QGIS vector layers, and UI feedback (import time label, selection highlighting, footer counters). Study area is implicitly Austria (BMN M34 CRS, 'KG' = Katastralgemeinde, 'EZ' = Einmessungszahl, 'BEV' = Bundesamt für Eich- und Vermessungswesen). Time range is not specified in the code logic; import timestamps are parsed from CSV headers but no global temporal filtering or analysis is performed.

desc: The script processes a user-provided suburb/locality shapefile and a text file defining administrative or functional zones (e.g., freight zones), each listing constituent suburbs. It performs spelling correction of suburb names using a custom letter-overlap heuristic (80% character match), harmonizes zone assignments to the suburb layer via attribute joining, splits the layer into per-zone suburb and dissolved boundary shapefiles, and programmatically generates georeferenced, labeled, and styled PDF map layouts (with legend, scalebar, north arrow, title) for each zone — all within QGIS Desktop (not GEE). The output consists of: (1) a modified suburb layer with 'Zone' attribute; (2) individual shapefiles per zone (suburbs + dissolved boundaries); and (3) publication-ready PDF (and PNG) maps per zone.

It transforms the input extent to EPSG:4674, intersects it with Brazilian state boundaries (BR_UF_2020.shp), constructs per-state WFS URIs (e.g., 'sicar_imoveis_ac' for Acre), and fetches only features intersecting the extent. name: Identify ecological value trees
desc: The script identifies individual trees with high ecological value (e.g., for retention as conservation trees — 'säästöpuut') within forestry cutting areas ('leimikko') in Finland. It integrates LiDAR-derived canopy height model (CHM) to detect tree tops, clips and samples raster layers (DTW — depth-to-water, Euclidean distance to water, vegetation zones, forest grid cells), joins tabular forest inventory attributes (fertility class, development class, stem counts, mean diameters/heights), and applies a weighted ecological scoring model (NP/phosphorus retention, BIO/biodiversity, LP/deadwood potential, DTW/moisture) to rank trees. Outputs are: (1) a point layer of ecologically scored trees ('Puiden ekologiset arvot'), styled with 'reTree3.qml'; and (2) a polygon layer aggregating these points into conservation area proposals ('Säästöpuuehdotus'), generated via point-to-area buffering ('point2area' with radius 1 m), styled with 'retreet_areas.qml'.

It does so by computing the geometric intersection (via union) between the two layers, calculating the area ratio of each intersected polygon relative to its original administrative-population polygon, scaling the population value proportionally by that ratio, and then aggregating (summing) the scaled values per mesh ID. The final output is a mesh layer with one attribute — 'snum' — representing the estimated total population (or other proportional quantity) assigned to each mesh unit.

desc: The script evaluates the altimetric (Z) positional accuracy of a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) by computing Z-discrepancies between reference ground control points (with known elevation values in a user-specified field) and interpolated DEM elevations at those point locations. It performs bilinear/bicubic/nearest-neighbor interpolation on the input raster DEM using GDAL, computes RMSE (Root Mean Square Error) of discrepancies, and classifies accuracy against Brazil’s Cartographic Accuracy Standard (PEC-PCD) across multiple map scales (1:500 to 1:250,000). Outputs include: (1) a vector layer with added 'discrep_Z' attribute containing per-point elevation differences; (2) an HTML report containing RMSE, descriptive statistics (mean, std, min, max), and a PEC-PCD compliance table mapping each scale to quality class (A–D or R). Input requirements are strictly a raster DEM layer and a point vector layer with a numeric elevation field — no satellite imagery, time-series, or classification logic is involved. All geospatial operations are local (point-in-raster sampling + interpolation), CRS validation is enforced (projected only), and no study area, time range, or external satellite data is referenced or used.

Output is a single-band GeoTIFF with NoData = -9999, preserving the input raster’s spatial reference, pixel size, and origin. desc: The script reconstructs the pre-erosion topographic surface for each lavaka (a type of gully landform common in Madagascar) by interpolating elevation values from random points sampled within user-defined pre-erosion surface polygons; it then computes the volumetric difference between this reconstructed surface and the current DEM (SRTM or TanDEM-X), producing clipped, lavaka-specific elevation-difference rasters and summary statistics (e.g., unique value reports) used to quantify eroded volume per lavaka.

desc: The script validates the geometric and attribute correctness of a user-provided cartographic grid (line layer) and grid numbering points (point layer) against a reference grid generated from a frame polygon and selected map scale (e.g., 1:5,000–1:250,000). It computes grid errors via symmetrical difference between reference and input grids, and identifies three types of point errors — missing points (present in reference but absent in input), incorrect points (mismatched 'numero' or 'direcao' attributes within tolerance), and extra points (present in input but not matched to any reference point within tolerance). Outputs are two error layers: a line layer of grid discrepancies labeled 'erro_grid', and a point layer of validation failures labeled 'ponto_faltante', 'ponto_incorreto', or 'ponto_extra', each retaining relevant attributes ('numero', 'direcao').

name: Detect oil palm tree canopy
desc: The script detects oil palm tree canopy locations in high-resolution raster imagery using a deep learning model (RetinaNet with ResNet101 backbone) trained specifically for small-object detection. It applies sliding-window inference (500×500 px windows, 470 px step) over the input GDAL raster, normalizes multispectral bands using 2nd–98th percentile scaling per band, performs inference, aggregates bounding boxes and scores, applies non-maximum suppression (IoU=0.3), and outputs vector geometries—either point (centroid), bounding box (polygon), or circle (diameter = bbox width)—with confidence scores as attributes. desc: The script generates a 3D polyline (LineStringZ) representing an arc derived from input 2D line geometries. name: Calculate vegetation quality index
desc: The script computes a composite Vegetation Quality Index (VQI) by integrating four ecological indicator layers derived from ESA CCI Land Cover and MaxNDVI Plant Cover composites: (1) Plant Cover Score (normalized and reclassified NDVI-based plant cover), (2) Erosion Protection Index (reclassified land cover classes mapped to erosion resistance levels), (3) Fire Risk Score (reclassified land cover classes mapped to fire susceptibility), and (4) Drought Resistance Score (reclassified land cover classes mapped to drought resilience). Each indicator is rescaled to a 1.0–2.0 continuous score via table-based reclassification; the final VQI is the geometric mean (fourth root of the product) of these four scores, producing a single raster representing integrated vegetation functional quality.

name: Compute network-based travel time raster
desc: The script computes a raster representing interpolated travel times across a geographic window, based on a linear network (e.g., roads or paths), using node-specific costs (i-cost and j-cost), directional flow constraints, lateral diffusion rules, and optional impassable barriers. It performs geometric proximity analysis (closest segment, buffering, distance-to-line), spatial discretization into a regular grid, per-pixel travel time accumulation (weighted by segment length ratio and sqrt(distance) × speed factor), and outputs two rasters: (1) a primary raster of computed travel times (in seconds or minutes, derived from speed in km/h and distance in meters), and (2) an auxiliary distance-to-network raster; both in ASCII Grid format with accompanying .prj and dictionary (.dic) files mapping individual values (e.g., station IDs). The algorithm operates entirely on vector input — no satellite or remotely sensed data is loaded, processed, or referenced. All parameters (e.g., radius, speed, pixel size) are user-defined at runtime; the study area, time range, and data sources are not embedded in the code.

desc: The script models the dispersion of an alien species along a hydrological network by delineating the total watershed upstream of a given occurrence point (using GRASS r.watershed and r.water.outlet), vectorizing stream networks and sub-watersheds, and clipping those features to the affected watershed. It outputs three vector layers: (1) the hydro network (streams) affected by the species, (2) the sub-watersheds intersecting the affected watershed, and (3) the full upstream watershed polygon derived from the occurrence point and DEM.

desc: The script computes the kilometerage range (e.g., '12+345 - 15+678') along a linear reference layer ('km', interpreted as a kilometer-marked linear infrastructure such as a road or rail alignment) that intersects with clipped and decomposed polygons representing investment areas ('inw'), buffered by a polygonal corridor ('pas'). Output is a vector layer ('WYNIK') enriched with 'wynik_km' (formatted kilometerage range or fallback 'km' field) and 'wynik_dist_pas' (distance from investment centroid to nearest km line).

name: Correct surface elevation model
desc: The script corrects an input raster surface (e.g., DEM or seismic horizon) using point-based control measurements (e.g., well tops or interpreted horizon picks), accounting for geological faults. It first samples the input raster at point locations to compute residuals (observed minus modeled elevation), then interpolates those residuals into a delta surface—constrained by fault lines via the custom 'PUMAplus:creategridwithfaults' algorithm—then adds the delta surface to the original to produce a fault-aware corrected surface. A quality control vector layer is generated containing both original residuals (Delta1) and post-correction residuals (Delta2) for validation. The study area, time range, satellite/sensor data, and specific geospatial parameters are not specified in the code; all inputs are user-provided layers (raster surface, point vector, fault lines), with no embedded temporal, geographic, or sensor metadata.

name: Aggregate flood hazard layers
desc: The script performs spatial upscaling (coarsening) of high-resolution flood modeling outputs—specifically DEM (digital elevation model), WSE (water surface elevation), and WSH (water surface height/depth)—using two physics-informed averaging methods from Bryant et al. (2023): (1) 'WSH Averaging', where WSH is directly averaged and WSE is reconstructed as DEM + WSH; and (2) 'WSE Averaging', where WSE is first averaged, then filtered against the coarsened DEM to retain only wet cells (WSE > DEM), and WSH is derived as WSE − DEM. Outputs are three coarsened rasters at user-specified scale: DEM_s2, WSE_s2, and WSH_s2, all aligned and consistent with hydrologic constraints.

name: Allocate mesh population to administrative boundaries
desc: The script performs a spatial disaggregation of population from statistical mesh polygons to administrative boundary polygons using area-proportional allocation. It first computes the area of each population mesh polygon, then unions the mesh layer with an administrative boundary layer (e.g., address/ward polygons), computes the area of each resulting intersection polygon, and calculates a proportional population value (dpop) for each intersection as: (intersection_area / original_mesh_area) × mesh_population. name: Aggregate administrative area by mesh
desc: The script performs spatial aggregation of administrative boundary polygons (INPUT) to mesh polygons (meshlayer) using area-proportional apportionment. It first computes the area of each administrative polygon, then unions it with the mesh layer to generate intersecting polygons. For each intersecting polygon, it calculates its area and the ratio of that area to the original administrative polygon's area. Using this ratio, it apportions (scales) a user-specified numeric field (aggrefield, e.g., population or area) from the administrative layer to the intersecting polygons. Finally, it aggregates (sums) the apportioned values by mesh ID (meshid field) and joins the aggregated results back to the original mesh layer, producing an output vector layer where each mesh polygon has an attribute (e.g., 'snum') representing the total apportioned value within that mesh.

name: Compute raster statistics in geosquare grids
desc: The script converts an input raster layer into a vector grid of equal-area geosquares (hierarchical H3-like or custom geohash-based polygons) aligned to a user-defined grid size (50 m to 10 km), clips the raster to a boundary polygon, and computes per-grid zonal statistics (Sum, Mean, Median, St Dev, Min, Max) for a selected raster band. name: Detect crop row gaps using spectral indices
desc: The script detects gaps in crop rows by first clipping a multispectral raster to a polygon mask, computing vegetation indices (NDI, ExG, TGI, NDVI) via band-wise normalization and raster algebra, binarizing the index output using adaptive thresholding and morphological operations, extracting plant centroid points from contours, and then counting detected plants within buffered line segments (e.g., crop rows) to compute gap-related metrics — specifically 'POCT' (plant count per row segment) and 'MEZV' (gap ratio: observed count / expected count, expressed as %) — written back to the input line vector layer's attribute table. Outputs include a classified binary raster, a point layer of all detected plant centroids, a filtered point layer of plants within row buffers, and updated line attributes quantifying row continuity.

name: Calculate line network tortuosity
desc: The script computes tortuosity (ratio of shortest-path distance to Euclidean distance) and shortest-path distances along a linear network (e.g., rivers, faults, or roads) between source points and optional target points. It constructs a NetworkX graph from an input linestring layer, optionally weighted by a numeric field (e.g., slope, resistance, or impedance), then solves shortest-path problems using Dijkstra's algorithm. Input requires a line layer (exploded into segments), a source point layer with 'ID' attribute, and an optional target point layer also with matching 'ID'. Output is a line vector layer where each segment represents an edge in the shortest path, attributed with source ID, accumulated path distance ('Distance'), and straight-line distance from first to last node ('SP_Dist'). No remote sensing data, time series, or satellite-derived inputs are used — all operations are vector-based geometric and graph-theoretic. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not specified in the code.

name: Calculate network service area
desc: The script computes service areas (isochrones) from a vector line network layer (e.g., roads) and a vector point layer of start locations, using graph-based shortest-path or fastest-path analysis. It builds a directed graph with configurable directionality (forward/backward/both), optional speed-based costing, topology tolerance, and outputs: (1) boundary nodes (points) representing reachable vertices within the travel cost threshold, including interpolated edge endpoints where the cost limit intersects edges, and (2) line segments representing all traversed network edges fully or partially within the cost limit. The script also optionally includes upper/lower bound points at cost-limit intersections on edges. No remote sensing data, time-series, or satellite-derived inputs are used — it operates purely on user-provided vector layers in QGIS Processing Framework. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geographic coordinates are not specified.

name: Calculate DEM difference
desc: The script computes the pixel-wise arithmetic difference between two input Digital Elevation Models (DEMs), supporting coordinate transformation when CRSs differ, resampling (nearest/bilinear/bicubic) during interpolation, and optional sign inversion. It outputs a GeoTIFF raster where each pixel value equals (Minuend − Subtrahend) or (Subtrahend − Minuend) depending on the selected reference grid, with NoData handling (-9999 default) and progress feedback. desc: The script extracts a comprehensive set of geospatial predictor variables for Urban Heat Island (UHI) modeling, including Land Surface Temperature (LST) from Landsat 9 Band 7, elevation (ALT), slope (PENTE), aspect/exposition (EXP), land cover (OCCSOL), soil type (NATSOL), tree height (HAUTA), hydrologic class (CATHYD), climatic zone (ZONECL), and urban-rural classification (URB), all sampled at LST pixel locations; it computes albedo (ALB) from Landsat 9 reflectance bands (LS1–LS6) and outputs a cleaned point vector table (CSV-compatible) with all attributes aligned to the same spatial extent and CRS (EPSG:4326), ready for machine learning input.

name: Remove alpha band from raster
desc: The script removes the 4th (alpha) band from a 4-band input raster (e.g., RGBA GeoTIFF), optionally converting transparent pixels (alpha = 0) to NoData values in the output 3-band RGB GeoTIFF. It reads the input via GDAL, validates that exactly 4 bands are present, extracts and interprets the alpha band as a binary transparency mask, applies it to set null values in RGB bands where alpha is zero, writes the result to a new GeoTIFF with proper geotransform and projection, and optionally loads the output into QGIS. The tool is designed for drone-derived or orthophoto rasters with embedded alpha channels — no satellite imagery, time-series, classification, or external geospatial analysis is performed.

name: Assess ecological priority scores
desc: The script performs a multi-layered spatial assessment of land parcels in Ontario, Canada, using QGIS Python processing to extract and summarize ecological, hydrological, soil, conservation, and species-at-risk attributes. name: Quantify fault overlap or separation distance
desc: The script computes the geometric relationship (overlap vs. separation) between two selected fault line features by constructing a quadrilateral buffer polygon from their transects, intersecting transect-derived lines with that polygon, measuring lengths and bearings of clipped segments, and statistically comparing mean bearing against mean fault strike to classify the interaction as 'Overlap' (O) or 'Separation' (S); outputs include clipped transect line layers labeled with depth, fault shorthand (e.g., 'CA_SF_O'), mean length, standard deviation, and a final polygon layer annotated with O/S ratio, average lengths, and total fault length.
